title: Travel & Sightseeing
description: Words for exploring Indonesia: temples and rice fields, islands and boats, tickets and guides, and the gifts you bring home.

items.registerNotes: Mostly in compounds: tempat wisata (a tourist attraction), wisata kuliner (a food tour). Berwisata, to go sightseeing, is a bit formal; people say jalan-jalan.
Turis asing (foreign tourist) and turis lokal (local tourist) are everyday words; wisatawan is the formal one in the news and on signs.
Casual, and usually not meant as an insult; the polite word is orang asing (foreigner).
items.cultureNote: Expect to hear it, along with Hello, Mister, from children and vendors. A friendly reply in Indonesian usually gets a delighted response.

items.registerNotes: Tiket masuk is an entry ticket; tiket pesawat and tiket kereta are plane and train tickets. Karcis is an older word still used for parking tickets.
Beli tiketnya di loket (Buy the ticket at the counter). Loket is any service window: at a station, a bank or a government office.
Pemandangannya indah sekali (The view is beautiful) is the stock compliment at any lookout or rice terrace.

items.cultureNote: Indonesia has more than 17,000 islands. Some names use the old word nusa instead: Nusa Penida, Nusa Tenggara.

items.pitfallNote: A candi is an ancient stone temple, like Borobudur and Prambanan in Java. A Balinese temple in use is a pura, a Chinese temple a klenteng, and a Buddhist one a vihara.
Pura-pura is a different word: to pretend.
items.cultureNote: Visitors wear a sarong and a sash, usually lent or rented at the gate, and keep their shoulders covered.

items.registerNotes: Literally plunging water: terjun is to jump or plunge, as in terjun payung (skydiving).
Rice terraces are sawah terasering. A dry field for other crops is a ladang.

items.english: gifts brought back from a trip
items.cultureNote: After a trip, family and colleagues expect oleh-oleh, usually a local food speciality like bakpia from Yogyakarta. Mana oleh-olehnya? (Where are my gifts?) is a half-joking welcome home.

items.registerNotes: Any place to stay, from a homestay to a small hotel. The verb is menginap, to stay the night: Menginap di mana? (Where are you staying?)

items.cultureNote: Hotels and phone shops ask to see or photocopy it (fotokopi paspor), so keep a copy handy.

items.registerNotes: Jadwal kereta (train timetable), jadwal dokter (a doctor's hours). Jadwalnya berubah means the schedule has changed.
Tujuannya ke mana? (Where are you headed?) At immigration, tujuan kunjungan is the purpose of your visit.
Perjalanannya berapa jam? (How many hours is the trip?) For a holiday, people say liburan or jalan-jalan instead.
Pemandu wisata is a tour guide; in tourist areas the English word guide is understood too.
Bisa tunjukkan di peta? (Can you show me on the map?) For a phone map, people just say Maps: Lihat di Maps saja.

items.english: scooter hire; to hire a scooter
items.registerNotes: Sewa motor sehari berapa? (How much is a scooter for a day?) Rates drop if you hire by the week or month.
items.cultureNote: Riding legally needs a motorbike licence (SIM) and a helmet, and police do stop tourists to check.

items.registerNotes: Naik kapal is to go by boat; kapal cepat is a fast boat, as to the Gili islands. A small wooden boat is a perahu.
Ferries and fast boats leave from the pelabuhan; ask Dari pelabuhan mana? (From which port?)
A desa wisata is a village that welcomes visitors. Kampung is also a village, but in a city it means a crowded neighbourhood, and kampung halaman is your home town.
Pusat kota is the city centre, and ke kota means going into town. In Jakarta, Kota on its own is the old town.

items.cultureNote: The busiest times are school holidays, Christmas and New Year, and above all Lebaran at the end of Ramadan, when millions travel home (mudik) and tickets sell out.
